question: A 67-year-old's hip pain has resisted several pills; he is referred for a hip replacement. Then an untried pill turns up. What would you advise?
answer: A second untried pill made more doctors try none. Each pill was a sensible next step alone, but picking between two is hard work, and referral offered a way out of the choice. Patients feel the same pull: a longer menu of treatments can end in doing nothing, or in taking the default.
move: When two good options stall you, compare each one with doing nothing.
ask: Which decision am I putting off only because I have two good options?

questions.prompt: One pill he hasn't tried. Start it, or just refer him?
Now there are two untried pills, both sensible. Start one, or just refer him?

scene.why: Picking between two good options is hard, so the easy way out is to pick neither.
scene.same: You held steady. The doctors didn't: no new pill rose from 53% to 72%.
scene.switched: You switched, like many doctors. A second good option made trying either one look harder.

reference: Redelmeier & Shafir, Medical decision making in situations that offer multiple alternatives, JAMA 273 (1995): 302-305
